title: Not everybody is “one-shotting’ their games…
author: dustandwater
selftext:
There is so much anti-AI sentiment, and so much auto-labelling everything that has any AI involvement “slop”. 

But so many of the comments that follow say things like, “if you’re just going to put two or three prompts into Claude and walk away” or “they just one-shot ChatGPT and call it a day”. 

But A) to the extent that this is the case, those games absolutely are shit and deserve no real respect, and B) many of the cases where people claim that’s what they did probably aren’t even true!

That aside, many of us aren’t doing that. I’m working on a piece of software at the moment, and my focus on this has made me out my game on the shelf for a while, because I don’t have the time to do both. 

I’ve been working on my App for around eight months now, spending around 5-hours a session, between three and five times a week, I’d estimate. That’s probably around 500–600 hours so far. And I’m probably 3/4 of the way done at this point. 

This is intensive planning and refining all the way, building each feature one-by-one, testing and debugging each one. It’s been a super involved process. I’m just not writing any code. 

I think people are quick to assume that ‘with AI’ automatically means no original thought, no real ownership. And I can’t be too mad: I see countless posts asking “what should I include in my game”. These people are literally crowdsourcing ideas that they’ll feed into Claude and then present a product as though it’s theirs. 

But I think many of us who use AI are equally unimpressed by those cases. Many of us aren’t doing that at all, we’re a million miles away from that.

replies.author: geanpn0
replies.body:
I'm following a similar path myself. I started working on my own survival game with some Satisfactory-style factory management elements and a few extra mechanics about two weeks ago.

During the first three days, I was mostly vibe coding everything, and progress was incredibly fast. That was until I reached a point where the game started struggling with the number of enemies I wanted on screen. So I decided to rebuild everything and switched to Godot, where I could prototype faster and felt more comfortable with the scripting language, since GDScript is quite similar to Python.

And it's honestly an insane amount of work. Using AI to create a game, no matter how simple it might seem, is extremely, extremely time-consuming.

There are days when I spend the entire day just thinking about and building a single system. And for that system to work, I need another system, which depends on another, and another, and another. I spend hours planning and implementing all of this, only to end the day with a character holding an axe. But at least I've built a solid foundation for everything I'll need in the future.

Architecture is also a huge part of it, and I think it's absolutely essential. Luckily, I'm already a software developer, so I'm familiar with these concepts. Even when I don't fully understand what the AI is doing to make the character move, I know that character movement belongs in a specific class, and I understand what each class should be responsible for.

But aside from architecture, I'd say the hardest part is actually creating a visual identity for your game. I'm not a particularly creative person, so I've really had to push myself in that area.

And then there's animation. God, animation is tedious. I've had to learn some Blender, manually fix hand positions, adjust animation frames, and ask AI to fill in the gaps, because AI alone just isn't enough.

You can't rely entirely on AI-generated assets. You'll have to fix textures, correct animations, adjust models, and do a lot of manual work.

When I started, I genuinely thought I'd have a decent prototype within a month. Now I'm thinking it'll probably take three or four months, maybe even longer, before I have something I'm happy with.

And that's considering I'm making a survival game that's primarily focused on factory management. It's a genre that relies heavily on gameplay mechanics and interconnected systems rather than visual presentation.

I can only imagine how much more work it would be for someone trying to create a game that's primarily focused on visuals, storytelling, and creative experiences. The amount of work involved in animations and 3D models alone must be enormous.

In my case, most of the work is really about designing mechanics and figuring out how all the systems should work together.

comments.author: Braindead_Games
comments.body:
I think a big issue that doesn't get discussed is the required knowledge the user should have when using AI. Yeah anyone can send a prompt and it'll pump out some type of content, but without trial and error, and guiding the AI in regards to what you're looking for you'll just get something generic. If the user doesn't know how to coordinate this information correctly, then yes you'll end up with slop. However, its its done correctly you can end up with a polished product. I also don't agree in dealing in absolutes regarding AI. If someone does most of the work from scratch but has the AI help with completion, then its automatically judged negatively. 

With that being said I do believe when using AI to generate graphics and such that its a cheap route to take. I can understand the frustration with that, because it could come off as soulless and not capture the feeling you're going for. I'm not necessarily against AI art, but i believe it to be more of a placeholder until a proper human artist can create the graphics needed.

I'm all for getting rid of the effortless slop/Asset Flips, but using a tool properly shouldn't have a negative impact.  
As time passes tools become more advanced. People don't seem to understand this.

replies.author: aeturnis-dev
replies.body:
I agree with 99% of this, but the AI generated assets I'd like to push back on, just a little. Yes, you can get slop assets that are obviously trash and incoherant and scream AI generated, but like with programming, or your agent programming, it takes iteration, tests, and willingness to say, "Yeah, that's shit." and move on and try something else. 

An example, I've been working on and shared with the community is working on a pipeline to animate cloth, headless with Claude and Blender. It' still early and needs work,  but you can get somewhere pretty decent now if you don't expect magic to happen from a single prompt.

https://reddit.com/link/1xg3p5i/video/rert4jdoyuxh1/player

It's not perfect, but that was accomplished without a human touching anything, and I think it's quite impressive, but it took a lot of work and research to get this.

replies.author: Braindead_Games
replies.body:
That's actually really neat. How long did it take you to put that together?

I probably should have used a different word than cheap. Inexpensive its probably a better fitting word. While yes AI can produced quality art after going through iterations, I feel like generating graphics is the biggest hurdle for AI. AI is really good at generating and compiling data, but when designing art from scratch most models struggle IMO. They may look flashy on the surface, but the patterns and such just don't look natural. Not saying AI art is inherently bad by any means, but good AI art definitely requires time for it to cook.

replies.author: aeturnis-dev
replies.body:
It took a couple of afternoons and some research and a lot of trial and error. Spring mechanics actually helped improve the cloth simulation, after doing some cross domain research, and I agree 100% that AI making art that is consistent and coherant is one if it's biggest challenges, and it's not surprising.

Art is intrinsically a human thing, and it can't see which, well, is a pretty big requirement for art, but AI can do math and measure and analyze data like a son of a bitch. I'm working on another pipeline with that idea in mind, so far it's promising but I haven't gotten to organic shapes or anything more complex than a chair or table.

It all depends on the effort, I guess that you put in.

https://i.redd.it/kjuzadjwavxh1.png

  
For the chair, I had Claude create one(the low poly) just on its own and then had it construct a Shaker style chair (A Met reference, free image) as if it were tasked with actually making a chair from cut and turned parts, slats and everything. The grain  texture is AI generated as well. Still refining the process. And it's not a fast process, to be clear.

replies.author: aeturnis-dev
replies.body:
I can't do art on a computer to save my life, so personally I find it easier for them to be generated. But there are certainly pro's and con's as you'll see, I had Claude write up how I do it, the following is directly from it:

>The generator builds wooden furniture the way a woodworker would (turned legs, mortise-and-tenon joints, bent slats, sawn boards), and it doesn't paint wood onto UVs. Each part gets its own virtual piece of lumber, and the wood is a 3D function of position inside it, baked into ordinary PBR textures. The grain always follows the construction, but up close it's more regular than real wood, and each object needs its own memory-hungry texture set.  
  
**How it works**  
  
**A grain frame per part** says which way the fibres run: along a turned leg's axis, a bent slat's curve, or a board's length.  
**A piece of stock per part,** from the object's seed: where the pith (the tree's centre) was, the ring spacing (1.6–3.2 mm) and a slight tone shift. Turned parts come from near the pith; boards and slats are flat-sawn, further out.  
**The wood is a 3D function.** Rings are the distance from the pith, wobbled by noise stretched along the fibres, with uneven widths, a darker latewood band, fibre streaks and a slow colour drift. Because it's 3D, end cuts show rings and long faces show stripes with no special cases, even inside the joints. End grain gets darker and rougher the more squarely a surface cuts across the fibres.  
**Bake to an atlas.** UVs come from the construction at uniform texel density, one 4096 px atlas per object. Each texel finds its triangle and evaluates the wood at that 3D point. The padding around each UV island holds the same 3D wood, so filtering across seams still samples real grain.  
**Plain PBR out:** base colour, roughness, and a normal map from a tiny height field (fibre texture and raised latewood, around 10 microns). Python/NumPy makes the textures, Blender just exports the glTF, and Godot 4 renders it with its standard material.  
**Smaller runtime versions** are downsampled from the master, each channel filtered for what it is (colour in linear light, normals averaged as vectors), then GPU-compressed.  
  
Solid 3D textures go back to the mid-80s (Perlin, Peachey), and Substance does procedural wood too, usually in UV space or projected onto the mesh. What this adds is the tie to the construction, with every part getting its own grain frame and log, plus automatic checks on the result.  
  
**Pros vs. scanned or tiling textures**  
  
**The grain follows the construction.** It bends with the slats, never flips at a UV seam, and every cut face shows end grain where it should. With a tiling texture you'd fix those by hand.  
**Every part is a different piece of wood,** so nothing visibly repeats across a set of chairs, and the same seed always gives the same wood.  
**The UV layout doesn't decide the grain.** Repacking the atlas moves the wood around in the texture, never on the model.  
**It scales to variants.** New chairs and tables need no texturing time, and the whole look is a few dozen numbers in a JSON file.  
**It's testable.** Same inputs, byte-identical textures (on   
the setups I've tested). The build rejects UV folds and overlapping texels, and a raking-light test in Godot checks the normal map against the bake's prediction (r = 0.99 on a striped diagnostic material; −0.99 with the green channel flipped).  
  
**Cons**  
  
**It looks procedural up close.** The long grain lines are more regular than real wood, especially on big surfaces, and there's no figure (curl, ray fleck), no knots, no defects and no wear. A good scan gets all of that for free.  
**Memory.** A unique 4096 px set per object is about 256 MiB of texture memory uncompressed (with mipmaps). At 2048 px with GPU compression it's about 11 MiB, with softer fine detail. A shared tiling material or trim sheet is far cheaper across a library.  
**Art direction is indirect.** You tune numbers instead of painting, so placing a knot just so, or wearing down the front rung where feet rest, is easy in Substance Painter and hard here.  
**Lots of upfront engineering:** UV generation, a rasterizer, and a tangent space that matches the engine's. For a single asset, buying a scan is faster.  
**It depends on the generator knowing the construction.** A sculpted or scanned mesh has no grain frames, so someone would have to author them.  
**One species so far.** Oak, for example, would need its pores and rays modelled.  
  
**vs. making textures by hand**  
  
Hand-authoring wins on character and storytelling, and it's faster for one hero asset. This wins on consistency and volume: any number of variants with correct grain and no texturing time, at the cost of looking a bit too perfect.

https://i.redd.it/r5oaiu8pnwxh1.png

comments.author: Blueberry_Gecko
comments.body:
I want to offer a talking point usually doesn't get discussed and is unfortunately a real "objective" downside to using AI, even ignoring all politics and ethics and even if you use it the very best way like you are.

It's the fact that people used to be able to tell at essentially a glance whether an art piece, whether it's a game/music/book, is good or not. You could read the first page of a book and if you notice the author is bad, you put it back on its shelf. That's not the case anymore because these low-level details are all covered by AI.

Unfortunately, as you know, an AI who writes perfect English doesn't magically give the prompter *good taste*, so a book can *look* really good but fall apart structurally after reading for 2 hours, because the prompter just didn't give a shit. The skill of writing used to be tightly coupled to writing something worth writing because who the hell would spend 10 years perfecting the low-level mechanics of sentence structure and POV and plot but not give a shit about writing a good story? All art is based on this trust relationship: You ask for my time and maybe money because you have something interesting to show.

AI has heavily increased the burden on the consumer. AI is being used by (some/quite many) people who don't give a shit but pretend that they care, just like children cheating on exams. People don't want to invest time and emotional energy into something no one cares about, but the problem is, it has become MUCH harder to tell because of this skill-vs-taste disconnect. This is tiresome, and by using AI you're unfortunately feeding into this. You're asking the consumer to perform a judgment that used to be trivial and now takes much more effort. Sometimes people smell the 'AI reek' from miles away and they just ignore the game completely, but sometimes it smells less or pops up only in the store page capsule and not in the Steam description. Now they have to make a difficult ballpark estimate on "does this author actually value my time and my money?".

Now, I'm preeetty sure that EVERYONE picks up on this subconsciously, because this is literally just signal vs. noise filtering, and brains are insanely good at this. Some people refuse to look at anything with the AI reek, which misses all 'bad writers but good storytellers who care very much' like you are, but it's imo a reasonable heuristic that avoids all the leeches. And my point is, you're not *entirely* innocent in this because you're using the reek and this is making it harder for people to tell.

replies.author: dustandwater
replies.body:
This is interesting, but I’m not convinced it applies at scale. 

Lazy AI can produce the illusion of quality in a 30-second video clip, maybe even a minute or more. But you can’t get a Hollywood movie out of AI with a few simple prompts. 

Written text can do sentences and paragraphs really well, but it’s pretty noticeably poor at telling stories convincingly. You wouldn’t really need to read for hours to tell that.

And the same is true for games. People can knock up a short gameplay trailer, but a playable full game is pretty quickly recogniseable as slop. 

In any of these media, it takes effort and care to produce quality, even with AI. 

However, there is still some currency in your argument. Because while there has always been low-effort ‘art’ (games: shovelware; books: pulp fiction; paintings: motel art) there has never been quite as much. And video games might be the worst of this. AI is allowing those looking for a quick buck to absolutely flood the market with low-effort, utter slop. So much that it threatens to completely drown out the quality games. 

But the funny thing is, those of us using AI to support our attempts to really make something good hate these slop factories just as much as the anti-AI brigade. We might even hate them more, because we hate being tarred with the same brush.

replies.author: Blueberry_Gecko
replies.body:
Absolutely, I agree with all you wrote. I didn't mean to say something about the quality of the result or that it takes no effort, only that it has become harder for consumers to look at it and go "this must be good" or "this looks like a highschool project".

That it takes a consumer hours of reading was probably a severe overstatement, you're right. It doesn't need to be hours though, probably even delaying this judgement by milliseconds would be enough to make them feel ever so slightly more tired and ever so slightly more annoyed, because people who care about quality are now asked to play the detective more than before.

Idk, I don't have any studies on the numbers obviously, it's just a feel I have that there is now a period of "neuronal overwhelm" where your brain is asked to filter noise in a way it hasn't before, and where there is a clear "adversary" trying to trick you into spending your attention. And perhaps some of this overwhelm will stay even after we've fully gotten used to it. (Not like this is particularly new with technology.)

Hopefully this all equalizes a bit when the market catches up and the money-grabbers drop out and people can go back to a baseline level of trust. Of course that depends on how AI develops.

comments.author: Protocontext

For me:

1) People who are against AI or who still think we're in GPT 3.5 and that AI is "a piece of junk that makes mistakes" don't have the mental capacity to accept that We're close to Skynet now, and AI is a powerful tool for accelerating development.
